title: Honi draws a circle (Taanit 23a)
hookLine: in drought, Honi draws a circle and won't step out until it rains

cards: Requests usually come padded. If it's not too much trouble. Only if you have time.
Totally fine if not. People shrink their requests so no one has to say no. Now picture a dry land in late winter.
The rains haven't come. Fields are cracking, cisterns are empty, and the people go to one man, known for his prayers: pray for rain. He does.
Nothing happens. So he draws a circle in the dirt around himself. Today, Honi, and a prayer that was anything but polite.

teach.h: I WON'T STEP OUT OF THIS CIRCLE.
teach.b: The story is in the Mishnah and the Talmud, tractate Taanit. Honi stands inside his circle and speaks to God. Master of the world, your children have turned to me, because I'm like a member of your household.
I swear by your great name, I won't move from this circle until you have mercy on your children.
A few drops fall. Honi says: that's not what I asked for. I asked for rain to fill the cisterns and the pits and the caves.
Now it pours, violent and frightening. Not that either, says Honi.

I asked for rain of goodwill, of blessing, of generosity. Then it rains the right way, steadily, until the people have to climb the Temple Mount to get out of the water, and they ask him to pray for it to stop.
The name stuck: Honi the circle-drawer. The great sage of the time, Shimon ben Shetach, sent him a message half scolding, half wonder. If you weren't Honi, I'd put you under a ban.

teach.h: LIKE A CHILD WITH A PARENT.
teach.b: You nag God like a child nagging his father, and his father gives him what he wants.
That's the heart of it. Honi isn't bargaining like a stranger. He's asking like family, boldly and specifically, and not taking drizzle for an answer.

how: Jewish prayer includes asking for rain in its season; from late fall until Passover a line for rain is added to the daily Amidah, and stories like Honi's are told about bold, personal prayer.

o: the sage who drew a circle and prayed for rain
a king who ordered a public fast in a drought
a prophet who called down fire on an altar

games.q: Honi's rain, three ways — tap the pairs.
p: you nag God like a child

s: Honi accepted the first drizzle gratefully
he said: that's not what I asked for.
Honi got his name from the circle he drew
Shimon ben Shetach praised Honi without reservation
he half scolded him, and half marveled that God answered like a father.

games.q: you've drawn the circle and prayed. a few drops fall, then stop. what do you say?
o: that's not what I asked for.
games.why: Honi said: not this, but rain to fill the cisterns. and later: not a flood, but rain of blessing. and it came.

practice: Picture a circle drawn around where you sit, and inside it name one thing you really want, for yourself or for someone else: not the polite version, the real, specific one, this person healing, this debt paid, this friendship mended.
If you pray, you can ask for it the way Honi did, like family; if not, simply say it clearly inside yourself and stay in the circle with it.

wordCard.voice: Honi, known ever after as the circle-drawer. In a drought he drew a circle, refused to step out until rain came, and then asked for the right rain.

carryVoice: Your line: draw the circle. Honi stayed in his circle until the right rain came. That's day two hundred seventy-seven.
